title: Ecce Dii tui Israel: plural form with singular sense; naming the image God means symbol, as papal ‘God the Father’ panels today
source_text: XXXIV. Neque est quod quis objiciat Jeroboam de vitulis a se consignatis dixisse, Ecce Dii tui Israel qui eduxerunt te de terra Aegypti, quod de vitulo aureo Israelitae jam in deserto dixerant. Etenim ex iis quae ante dicta sunt patet, primo verba quamvis sint pluralis numeri, sensum tamen ibi habere singularem, secundum linguae Hebraicae genium, & frequentem Scripturae usum. Deinde nomen Dei vitulis illis tribui, quia Dei symbola & imagines erant, non quod crederentur in se esse numen illud ipsum, quod antequam formarentur, Israelitas ex Aegypto miraculose eduxerat. Quemadmodum hodie, qui imaginem quandam habitu imperiali vel Papali effictam, dicunt esse Deum Patrem, non propterea credunt imaginem istam, sine ulla figura, & ad litteram esse Deum Patrem, sed solum ejus symbolum & repraesentationem.
pass_a_gloss: Nor is there reason for anyone to object that Jeroboam said of the calves cast by himself, Behold thy Gods, O Israel, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt, which the Israelites had already said of the golden calf in the desert. For from those things which were said before it is plain, first that the words, although they are of the plural number, yet have there a singular sense, according to the genius of the Hebrew tongue, and the frequent use of Scripture. Next that the name of God is attributed to those calves, because they were symbols and images of God, not because they were believed to be in themselves that very divinity which, before they were formed, had miraculously led the Israelites out of Egypt. Just as today, those who say that a certain image fashioned with imperial or Papal habit is God the Father do not therefore believe that that image, without any figure, and to the letter, is God the Father, but only his symbol and representation.
pass_b_english: Plural Dii on the calves tracks Hebrew idiom, not a pantheon.
Calling the symbol God mirrors modern panels labeled God the Father—representation, not literal identity.
